problem.statement: Improvement campaigns spend their budget on whatever is reported most often. Frequent complaints that were never verified, and fixes that would have failed a cheap check, consume budget that higher-value problems needed.

hypothesis: If the improvement process ranks problems by verified failures times severity per unit of cost, pilots a built fix on observed cases before paying for a held-out evaluation, and stops when no remaining problem is worth its cost, then with the same budget on unseen failure episodes it will deliver more independently validated harm reduction and spend less on experiments that fail.
expected_benefit: More validated harm reduction per fixed experiment budget; lower cost of failed experiments.
possible_regressions: Pilots cost budget that could have funded another submission
A problem with few verified failures but high latent harm is ranked low

change.summary: Replaces the frequency-first improvement policy with an expected-value policy: prioritization, a pilot step, pruning and a stopping rule all change.

Without the unverified complaint class the advantage is not demonstrated (difference 5.6167, 95% interval -5.15 to 16.65)
limitations: The arena is a synthetic testbed. Its failure distribution is invented and its fix library stands in for hypothesis generation; the result describes behaviour in this testbed, not improvement rates in real work.
By construction the arena contains a frequently reported, never verified complaint class. The comparison is repeated without it as a sensitivity check; only the main comparison decides.
Policies and validators are deterministic, so each episode is run once. The interval reflects which episodes were drawn.
Both policies were written by the same author who built the arena.
justification: Accepted: validated_benefit improved by 12.6167 against the incumbent (95% interval 0.4167 to 25.4333) with every hard gate passed.
